result:
My favorite invention is the space between words.

For most of antiquity, Greek and Latin were written without it. Text ran in an unbroken stream of letters, called scriptio continua, and the reader's job was to find the words inside it. The Romans had word dividers for a while, small dots placed between words, and then gave them up around the second century, apparently in imitation of the Greeks. It's one of the few cases I know of where a writing system was made harder to read on purpose.

This worked because reading was mostly done aloud. You sounded out the stream, and your ear did the parsing your eye couldn't. Speech has no reliable gaps between words either, and fluent listeners manage fine, so a Roman hearing his own voice would recognize the words as they went by.

Then Latin arrived in Ireland, where nobody spoke it natively. Irish monks in the seventh and eighth centuries were learning it from books, as a foreign language, and the ear trick fails if you don't already know what the words sound like. So they started leaving gaps. The habit spread through Britain and then slowly across the continent, taking a few centuries to become standard. The historian Paul Saenger has argued that this is what made silent reading routine, and with it much of what we now think reading is: fast, private, and skimmable. You could read something heretical without anyone hearing you.

I like two things about this story. The first is that the invention is made of nothing. Nobody had to design a symbol, only to stop writing for the width of a letter. It may be the most useful blank in history, with zero as its only real competitor.

The second is who invented it. Native speakers never needed the space, so they never thought of it. The people who found the text hard were the ones who fixed it, and the fix turned out to be better for everyone, including the fluent. Curb cuts were built for wheelchairs and are used by everyone with a stroller or a suitcase, and subtitles were made for deaf viewers and are now left on by half the people I talk to. The experts in a system are often the last to see what's wrong with it, because their skill covers for the flaw.

This piece has several hundred of those gaps in it, and I'd guess you didn't notice a single one.
